::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**The list this page specifies is compiled and ranked by Claude, not by
Andy.** An agent runs once a month, finds public pharmacometrics skill files,
scores each one against the criteria in Section 4, and publishes the result.
Andy sets the criteria and their weights in a criteria file (Section 5). He does
not choose entries, adjust scores, or review the ranking before it is
published. The list page carries the same statement at its top (Section 7).
:::

## 1. Goal

A public list of pharmacometrics skill files, grouped into three categories and
ranked within each by a score computed from stated criteria. An agent updates
it every month. Every score links to the commit it was measured on and to the
evidence behind each part of it, so a reader or a skill's author can check it.

A private review on 2026-10-02 did this once, by hand. It found eleven libraries
across twelve repositories and scored each on four judged components: people
and provenance (35), output quality and verification (40), pharmacometrics
relevance (15), and maintenance and usability (10). This specification keeps
that shape and replaces each judged score with a measurement where one exists,
or with a fixed yes-or-no rubric where it does not.

The list connects to [Specification 1](specification1-make-skill-files.qmd) in
two directions. The list is where the first skill looks for material to borrow,
and where that skill will eventually be listed. Specification 1's test cases, in
turn, become the quality benchmark for the model evaluation category
(Section 4.1).

### Out of Scope

- **Endorsement.** A rank says how a skill scored on these criteria. It says
  nothing about whether the skill is fit for a given analysis on real data.
- **Software without a skill file.** MCP servers, R packages and
  pharmacometrics software are listed only if they ship a skill file.
- **Judging people.** The expertise score measures a publication record found
  in OpenAlex. A low score means no record was found, not that the author lacks
  expertise.

## 2. What Is Listed

### The Unit Is a Skill

A skill is one skill file, the `SKILL.md` an assistant loads together with the
reference files beside it. A library contributes one entry per skill that passes
inclusion. To keep a library of 150 skills from filling a category, at most
three skills per library are ranked in each category. The library's other
skills in that category are listed under its highest-ranked entry, unscored.

### Inclusion Criteria

A skill is listed when all four hold:

1. **Public.** It is readable at a stable URL on GitHub, GitLab or Codeberg.
2. **Loadable.** It is a `SKILL.md` with `name` and `description` in its
   frontmatter, or an equivalent instruction file that declares when an
   assistant should load it.
3. **Pharmacometric.** It names at least one tool or task from Section 3. The
   agent finds candidates by keyword match and confirms each by reading the
   skill.
4. **Not a copy.** A skill whose text matches an already-listed skill by more
   than 80%, by line-level comparison, is merged into that entry as a copy.

An archived repository is listed and flagged, and its maintenance score is 0.

## 3. Categories

Every skill sits in exactly one category and carries tags for the tools and
tasks it covers.

| Category | A skill belongs here when | Examples of coverage |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **Tool skills** | Most of its instructions would be wrong or useless for a different piece of software | NONMEM, PsN, Monolix, nlmixr2 and rxode2, mrgsolve, Pumas, PKNCA, Phoenix WinNonlin, PK-Sim, Simcyp, Jinkō |
| **Task skills** | Its instructions hold across tools, even when its code examples use one | Exploratory data analysis and dataset assembly, structural model building, covariate modeling, model evaluation and diagnostics, simulation and trial design, NCA, exposure-response, PBPK and QSP, report writing, document review |
| **Evaluation resources** | It measures how well an assistant does pharmacometrics work rather than instructing it | Test cases with expected findings, benchmarks, judging rubrics |

: The three categories {tbl-colwidths="[18,40,42]"}

When the test does not decide between tool and task, the skill goes under task
and carries the tool as a tag. The page also offers a view by tag, so a reader
looking for everything on nlmixr2 finds both its tool skills and the task skills
written for it.

**Evaluation resources are the third category** because the quality criterion
needs them. They are the only direct measure of whether a skill helps
(Section 4.1), so the list tracks them as closely as the skills. The
alternative considered was a workflow category, for libraries that chain many
skills into an end-to-end analysis. It was rejected because a workflow is
better described by its tags than by a category of its own.

## 4. Ranking Criteria

Four scores, each from 0 to 100, combined by weights from the criteria file.

| Score | Measures | Measured from | Default weight |
|:---|:---|:---|---:|
| **Q**, quality | Whether the skill's guidance is sound, sourced and verified | Rubric, error audit, verification checks; a benchmark where one exists | 45 |
| **E**, expertise | The authors' publication record in pharmacometrics | OpenAlex | 25 |
| **M**, maintenance and usability | Whether the skill is kept up to date and can be installed and reused | GitHub API and repository files | 20 |
| **A**, adoption | Whether others use it | GitHub stars and forks | 10 |

: The four scores {tbl-colwidths="[22,34,30,14]"}

Andy's three proposed criteria map to Q, M and E. Influence can mean who wrote a
skill or who uses it, and those measure different things, so it is split into E
and A. The 2026-10-02 review's relevance component is now the inclusion rule in
Section 2, because a skill that is not pharmacometric does not belong on the
list at any score.

### 4.1 Quality

Quality is the hardest of the four to measure. The only direct measure is a
benchmark: run an assistant on test cases with known answers, with and without
the skill, and count the difference. Benchmarks exist for almost no
pharmacometrics task yet, so Q starts from a rubric and an error audit, and a
benchmark joins them where one becomes available.

**The rubric.** Ten yes-or-no items. A *yes* needs a quoted line from the skill
as evidence; an item answered without a quote scores *no*. Items that do not
apply to a skill are left out of its denominator.

| # | Item | Applies to |
|:---|:---|:---|
| R1 | States what the skill does not do | All |
| R2 | Cites sources: at least 5 of 10 randomly sampled recommendations name a published source or official documentation | All |
| R3 | Says what to do when a check fails, beyond listing which checks to run | Task |
| R4 | Qualifies numeric thresholds such as shrinkage, RSE or condition number with context, or gives none | Task |
| R5 | Ties the depth of evaluation to the model's intended use | Task: model building and evaluation |
| R6 | States the limitations of its own output | All |
| R7 | Gives code examples complete enough to run | Skills with code |
| R8 | Runs those examples in continuous integration | Skills with code |
| R9 | Continuous integration passes on the pinned commit | Skills with code |
| R10 | Stores outputs from a real run | Skills with code |

: The quality rubric {tbl-colwidths="[8,70,22]"}

R3 to R5 are the three levels of the 2026-10-02 review turned into items. A
skill that only generates plots scores none of them. A diagnostic checklist
scores R3. A skill that reads diagnostics the way a scientific reviewer would
scores all three.

**The error audit.** A second pass, by a different model from the one that
scored the rubric, reads the skill adversarially and lists every statement it
judges wrong. Each finding quotes the line, gives the reason, and cites a
source.

- A *major* error would lead an assistant to a wrong modeling decision. The
  2026-10-02 review found two: a rule that turns an ETA shrinkage threshold into
  a decision to fix the variance, and a population PK example whose variance
  parameters never enter the objective function.
- A *minor* error is wrong but would not change a decision.

$$
Q_{\rm rubric} = 100 \times \frac{\text{items met}}{\text{items applicable}},
\qquad
Q = \max\left(0,\ Q_{\rm rubric} - 25\,n_{\rm major} - 5\,n_{\rm minor}\right).
$$

**The benchmark, where one exists.** When an evaluation resource covers a
skill's task with test cases that carry expected findings, run an assistant on
those cases twice, with and without the skill, and take the share of expected
findings each run reports:

$$
Q_{\rm bench} = 50 + 50\,(\text{recall}_{\rm with} - \text{recall}_{\rm without}),
$$

so 50 means the skill made no difference, and less than 50 means it made the
assistant worse. Where $Q_{\rm bench}$ exists, the reported quality is the mean
of the two: $\tfrac12 Q + \tfrac12 Q_{\rm bench}$. The first benchmark expected
is Specification 1's test cases for model evaluation in nlmixr2.

**Judging reliability.** The rubric is scored twice on the same commit, in
independent runs. Where the two runs disagree on an item, a third run decides.
Each month's page reports the share of items on which the first two runs
agreed. If that share falls below 85% for an item, the item's wording is
ambiguous, and the run reports it to Andy as a proposed change to the criteria.

### 4.2 Expertise

Andy proposed the total Google Scholar impact of all authors. Google Scholar has
no public API, its terms forbid automated querying, and many pharmacometricians
have no profile there. OpenAlex is a free, open index of scholarly works with an
API, author records linked to ORCID identifiers, citation counts and subject
topics, and it is the source here.

Four ways to turn a publication record into a score:

| Method | Computed as | Drawback |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Sum of h-indices | Sum over all contributors | Rewards a long author list over the person who wrote the skill |
| Maximum h-index | The highest among contributors | Credits a senior name who may have touched one line |
| Total citations | Sum of all contributors' citations | Dominated by one highly cited paper, often outside pharmacometrics |
| **Share-weighted field h-index** (default) | Each contributor's h-index over their pharmacology and pharmacokinetics works, weighted by their share of the skill's lines | Needs a commit history; a skill committed by one account under an organization name scores 0 |

: Ways to score expertise {tbl-colwidths="[26,38,36]"}

The default proceeds in four steps.

1. **Contributors and shares.** Each contributor's share is the fraction of
   lines in the skill's files that they last changed, from the commit history.
   Where the repository names its authors in a `CITATION.cff`, `AUTHORS` or
   `DESCRIPTION` file, those authors share equally instead.
2. **Identity.** A contributor is matched to an OpenAlex author only with
   evidence: an ORCID on their GitHub profile or in `CITATION.cff`, or a name
   and affiliation that agree between the two. The evidence is recorded. A
   contributor without a match scores 0 and is labelled *not found*.
3. **Field h-index.** For each matched author, $h_{\rm PMx}$ is the h-index
   computed over their works in OpenAlex's pharmacology and pharmacokinetics
   topics only. This keeps a highly cited author from another field from
   scoring as a pharmacometrician.
4. **Score.** With $s_c$ the share of contributor $c$ and a cap of 25,

$$
E = 100 \times \min\left(1,\ \frac{\sum_c s_c\, h_{{\rm PMx},c}}{25}\right).
$$

### 4.3 Maintenance and Usability

$$
M = \tfrac12\,\text{Recency} + \tfrac12\,\text{Usability}.
$$

**Recency** is $100 \times \max(0,\ 1 - d/365)$, where $d$ is the number of
days since the last commit to the skill's own files, not to the repository. An
archived repository has $M = 0$.

**Usability** is 20 points for each of five checks:

1. An open-source licence approved by the Open Source Initiative (OSI).
2. Valid frontmatter, with `name` and `description`.
3. Installation instructions.
4. Dependencies stated, with versions.
5. A version tag or release.

A skill without a licence is listed with a ⚠️ flag, because it cannot legally be
reused, whatever its other scores.

### 4.4 Adoption

$$
A = 100 \times \frac{\ln(1 + \text{stars} + \text{forks})}{\ln(1 + \max_{\rm category}(\text{stars} + \text{forks}))}.
$$

Stars and forks count at repository level, so every skill in a large library
shares that library's adoption score, and stars can be bought. The default
weight is low for both reasons, and the criteria file can set it to 0.

### 4.5 Total Score and Ties

$$
S = \frac{\sum_i w_i X_i}{\sum_i w_i}, \qquad X \in \{Q, E, M, A\}.
$$

A score that does not apply to a skill, such as the benchmark part of Q, is
left out and the weights are renormalized. A score that applies but could not be
measured counts as 0 and is flagged; it is never imputed.

**Ties.** Skills within 5 points of each other share a rank.

**Rank range.** Each skill is also ranked under two other weightings, quality
alone and equal weights, and the page shows the range of its ranks across the
three. A skill ranked 2nd under the defaults and 2nd to 4th across all three is
reported as "2 (2–4)".

## 5. The Criteria File

`criteria.yml`, in this folder, is the only file Andy edits. The agent reads it
at the start of every run, and the list page states which version of it each
month's ranking used. A change takes effect from the next run.

``` yaml
version: 1
weights:
  quality: 45
  expertise: 25
  maintenance: 20
  adoption: 10
tie_margin: 5
max_ranked_per_library_per_category: 3
categories: [tool, task, evaluation]
quality:
  rubric: [R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, R6, R7, R8, R9, R10]
  penalty: {major: 25, minor: 5}
  benchmark_share: 0.5
  min_judge_agreement: 0.85
expertise:
  method: share_weighted_field_h   # or sum_h, max_h, total_citations
  h_cap: 25
maintenance:
  recency_horizon_days: 365
adoption:
  enabled: true
```

The rubric's wording lives in a second file, `rubric.md`, so an item can be
reworded without changing its number. The agent never edits either file. It
proposes changes in its monthly report, and Andy makes them.

## 6. The Monthly Run

A Claude Code routine, scheduled on the first of each month, runs these steps
in a cloud session against this repository.

1. **Known-answer checks.** Score two fixtures first: the skills with the two
   major errors found on 2026-10-02, pinned at the commits where those errors
   were found. If the error audit misses either error, stop and report without
   publishing. A scorer that cannot find a known error should not be ranking
   anything.
2. **Discovery.** Run the fixed queries in `discovery.yml`: GitHub code search
   for `SKILL.md` files containing the tool and task names in Section 3; GitHub
   topics such as `agent-skills` and `claude-skills` combined with
   pharmacometrics terms; known indexes, including the ISoP AI/ML SIG Agentic
   Workflows repository; and links in the year's ACoP and PAGE abstracts.
   Record each query with its number of hits, candidates and inclusions.
3. **Snapshot.** Pin every listed skill to a commit SHA. Everything that month
   is scored against that commit.
4. **Scoring.** Recompute M and A for every skill every month. Recompute Q only
   for skills whose files changed since the last run. Recompute E every three
   months, or when the contributors change.
5. **Changes.** Give a one-line reason for every skill that moved three or more
   places, or whose score changed by 10 or more points.
6. **Publishing.** Write `list/YYYY-MM.yml`, update the list page from it,
   render the site, and open a pull request with the report as its
   description. The pull request merges without review once the site renders
   and the privacy check passes (decision 1).

The cloud session has no access to the private name lists the commit hook
reads, so it needs the `PRIVATE_NAMES` and `SENSITIVE_TOPICS` variables
described in `CLAUDE.md`. OpenAlex asks API users for a contact address; set
one in the routine's environment rather than in the code.

Rubric scoring and the error audit cost model time on every new or changed
skill. Unchanged skills keep their quality score, so after the first run the
monthly cost follows the rate at which skills change, not the length of the
list.

## 7. The List Page

`curated-list.qmd`, in this folder, renders from the latest data file through
Quarto listings of `type: table`, one listing per category. Listings read YAML
without running code, so the page has nothing to freeze and nothing that needs
R on the publishing runner.

| Column | Contents |
|:---|:---|
| Rank | Shared on ties, with the rank range in brackets |
| Skill | Name, linked to the pinned commit |
| Library | Repository |
| Tags | Tools and tasks |
| S, Q, E, M, A | The total and the four scores |
| Flags | ⚠️ no licence · ⚠️ archived · ❌ major error found · ⚠️ authors not found in OpenAlex |
| Evidence | Link to the skill's evidence: rubric quotes, audit findings, matched OpenAlex records with each author's field h-index, API values |

: Columns of the list page {tbl-colwidths="[18,82]"}

The page opens with this statement, verbatim:

> This list is compiled and ranked each month by Claude, an AI model made by
> Anthropic, running unattended. No person reviews the entries or the scores
> before they are published. Andy Stein sets the criteria in
> [Specification 2](specification2-curated-list.qmd) and does not adjust
> individual scores. A score measures what the criteria measure; a high rank
> is not an endorsement for use on real data. Authors who find an error can
> open an issue on GitHub.

Each month's data file stays in `list/`, so the page can show how a skill's
rank has changed.

## 8. Checking the Method

- **Test and retest.** Score the same snapshot twice, in independent runs. The
  rank correlation between the two runs is reported each month. Below 0.9, the
  ranking is noise at the resolution the page displays.
- **Known answers.** The fixtures in step 1 of Section 6.
- **Comparison with the 2026-10-02 review.** On the first run, compare the top
  three in each category with the hand review's ranking. Agreement is a sanity
  check, not a target: the hand review used judged scores this method replaces.
- **Weight sensitivity.** The rank range in Section 4.5.

## 9. Decisions

Andy's answers on 2026-10-07 to the questions this section first carried.

1. **The monthly pull request merges without review.** Andy's veto is the
   criteria file, not the ranking.
2. **The page shows individual h-indices.** The evidence for each skill lists
   every matched author with their field h-index and OpenAlex record.
3. **The default weights stand**: quality 45, expertise 25, maintenance 20,
   adoption 10.
4. **Individual skills are ranked**, for now, under the per-library cap in
   Section 2. Ranking libraries may replace this later.
5. **Authors are not told** when their skill is listed. The agent makes no
   contact outside this repository.

## 10. First Steps

1. Write `criteria.yml` and `rubric.md` with the defaults above.
2. Build the two fixtures from the 2026-10-02 review.
3. Run the method once in an ordinary Claude Code session, on the eleven
   libraries from that review plus a fresh discovery pass, scoring each
   snapshot twice to measure agreement.
4. Build `curated-list.qmd` from the first data file, and confirm that Quarto
   table listings read the YAML as Section 7 assumes.
5. Schedule the monthly routine.
